scope: Independent source-access audit, jewish-tradition episodes 18–30. Repository not modified.

episodes.dateClaim: 4th c. CE; archaeological range, not an exact dedication

sources.consulted: Object record, description, dating and site fields
sources.locator: Mosaic panels / dating fields; catalogue item 233 (related Hammath Tiberias record)
sources.supports: A synagogue mosaic includes a zodiac with Helios, seasons and sanctuary imagery; catalogue dates this item 286–337 CE.
sources.limits: This is a related CJA record, not source-list item 644. Catalogue dating differs in precision from broad Late Roman/Byzantine archaeological summaries; do not generalize one floor's imagery into uniform communal belief.

sources.supports: Moshe Dothan's 1961–63 excavations; decorated synagogue floor with zodiac, menorah/ritual objects and inscriptions in multiple languages.
sources.limits: Page uses broad Late Roman/Byzantine dating; it does not establish a precise dedication year or explain the community's theology.

episodes.assessment: Keep date explicitly approximate; report the disagreement between catalogue and broad archaeological range.

episodes.place: Dio-Caesarea (Sepphoris); wider Galilee/Palestine in later accounts

sources.supports: Search excerpt reports Gallus' troops defeated the insurgents and destroyed Dio-Caesarea.
sources.limits: Do not claim full passage consultation. A later Christian account, not contemporary local testimony.

sources.type: late antique Roman narrative (Ammianus, contextual only)
sources.limits: Not evidence for the 351/352 revolt.

sources.locator: Entry heading and source attribution to Sozomen HE 4.7
sources.supports: Identifies a later account of the revolt.
sources.limits: Search excerpt only, not read as full article.

episodes.assessment: Event/revolt is attested by later Christian historians; exact scale, casualties, sequence, and whether the whole city was razed require source-by-source qualification. No civilian evacuation episode independently verified.

episodes.dateClaim: c.350–400 CE as a broad editorial period
episodes.place: Galilee; compilation is not securely located at one site

sources.type: academic chapter (abstract only in prior source list)
sources.consulted: Abstract only; full chapter not accessed
sources.locator: Abstract on rabbinic literature and society
sources.supports: General scholarly context only.
sources.limits: Abstract does not verify a precise compilation date, place, or uninterrupted institutional record.

sources.consulted: Relevant excerpt read via hosted thesis; exact full bibliographic landing page not captured in this audit
sources.locator: Excerpt discussing traditional c.425 Yerushalmi date and conflation of evidence
sources.supports: Warns that dating the Jerusalem Talmud and the patriarchate's end is debated and not directly fixed by a contemporary dated witness.
sources.limits: A thesis argument is secondary scholarship; it does not itself establish an alternative exact date.

episodes.assessment: Describe a multigenerational textual process, not a dated one-time event; c.350–400 is a framing range, not a documented closure.

sources.supports: Ammianus says Julian planned at great expense to restore the Jerusalem temple and entrusted the task to Alypius of Antioch; reports fiery events near the foundations that halted work.
sources.limits: The flames and their effects are Ammianus' account, not independently established natural or miraculous cause. This passage alone does not establish a formal surviving imperial edict, completed work, or the local community's response.

episodes.assessment: Attribute supernatural explanation to Ammianus; report an attempted project, not a completed restoration.

episodes.place: Thessalonica (law addressed to the praetorian prefect)

sources.type: later legal-code English translation of imperial constitution
sources.supports: Prohibits a Jew marrying a Christian woman and a Christian man marrying a Jewish woman; classifies such a union as adultery and permits public accusation.
sources.limits: Normative law, not evidence of prevalence or enforcement in Thessalonica or elsewhere; the surviving text is transmitted in a later code.

episodes.assessment: Keep the law's scope and penalty distinct from claims about actual marriages or local community behavior.

episodes.place: Constantinople; order directed to eastern military officials

sources.locator: CTh 16.8.9, lines 817–818 in opened transcript; address and date in heading
sources.supports: States Jewish worship is not prohibited by law; notes assemblies interdicted in some places; orders officials to restrain those who under Christian name destroy/loot synagogues.
sources.limits: The law records the emperor's norm and asserted problem, not general compliance or a universal guarantee of safety. 'Some places' does not identify all localities.

episodes.assessment: Preserve both protection against synagogue destruction and the stated local restrictions on assemblies; neither erases the other.

episodes.dateClaim: Late antiquity; dating disputed (proposals range from early 3rd to 5th c.; 4th c. also argued)

sources.consulted: Inscription record and displayed Greek text read
sources.supports: Text preserves a list including names and labels such as theosebēs; it is an epigraphic community-related record.
sources.limits: Database text alone does not settle date, precise membership status, or whether listed names are donors, officials, or a census.

sources.consulted: Site description and inscription summary read
sources.supports: Describes a 2.8m inscribed column with lists on two faces; gives approximate counts and association with synagogue/donors.
sources.limits: The page cautions through its summary that categories are complex; names list is not a population census. Dating remains debated.

sources.consulted: Abstract/search excerpt only; full article not accessed
sources.locator: Gary Gilbert, 2004, discussion of inscription's dating debate
sources.supports: Reports early-third-century initial publication and later fourth/fifth-century proposals; article argues an alternative fourth-century dating.
sources.limits: Only abstract/extract consulted; do not state the paper's full argument as read.

episodes.assessment: Treat inscription as primary evidence for named persons/categories; label date and meaning contested.

episodes.place: Milan; directed to praetorian prefect Messala

sources.supports: Directs that sums already collected by patriarchal agents go to the imperial treasury and ends their future collection/transmission in the described form.
sources.limits: A targeted fiscal rule addressed to a named official; does not prove instant compliance everywhere or the end of all Jewish communal contributions.

episodes.assessment: Do not turn a fiscal transfer into a universal claim about community finance or office abolition.

episodes.dateClaim: Construction late 4th–early 5th c.; mosaic phases need separate dating

sources.type: peer-reviewed archaeological/radiocarbon study, open full text
sources.consulted: Abstract, introduction, results and conclusion read
sources.supports: Controlled excavation, pottery and radiocarbon place synagogue construction with high probability in late 4th–early 5th c.; authors warn calibration/site-formation issues limit precision and distinguish later fills from original use.
sources.limits: Dates construction, not automatically every mosaic panel or a single dedication. Authors stress limitations of radiocarbon samples and later rebuilding/raising of floor.

sources.consulted: Search-result abstract only; full report not opened in this audit
sources.supports: Excavation revealed a Late Roman synagogue with figural mosaics, including Samson imagery.
sources.limits: Only abstract/search-result text consulted, so no panel-level chronology claimed.

episodes.assessment: A synagogue with monumental mosaic floor is supported; keep construction and decoration sequence distinct and avoid claiming the Samson panel dates exactly to c.400.

episodes.place: Rome; order addressed to Italian praetorian prefect

sources.supports: Revokes the prior order withholding customary payments Jews sent to regional patriarchs and permits them again under older imperial statutes.
sources.limits: A legal permission/administrative reversal does not demonstrate actual remittance or restore every aspect of patriarchal authority.

episodes.assessment: Describe reinstatement of a particular customary transfer, not broad repeal of all restrictions.

episodes.place: Constantinople; order to eastern praetorian prefect

sources.supports: Removes Gamaliel's honorary prefecture insignia; restricts building new synagogues; permits destruction of abandoned synagogues subject to no-sedition condition; bars him from judging Christian cases and routes disputes to provincial governors.
sources.limits: The text does not explicitly abolish the patriarchate or report Gamaliel's death. It combines restrictions with conditional procedural rules; do not infer universal enforcement.

episodes.assessment: The date is 20 October in the primary transcript; some modern summaries give a different day. This law alone does not prove office ended in 415.

episodes.dateClaim: 15 February and 9 April 423 CE; separate constitutions

sources.supports: CTh16.8.25 (15 Feb) protects old synagogues from arbitrary confiscation and provides restoration/remedy for specified appropriated sites, while §25.2 bars new synagogues and says existing ones remain. CTh16.8.26 (9 Apr) separately prohibits injury/occupation/burning of synagogues and includes severe penalties in a distinct conversion/circumcision provision. CTh16.8.27 (8 Jun) again bars new synagogues while protecting existing ones.
sources.limits: These are distinct laws and scopes; do not merge them into a single blanket protection or persecution policy. Legal texts do not prove local enforcement.

episodes.assessment: Retain the coexistence of protection for existing property and restrictions on new construction; identify which provision supports each claim.

episodes.dateClaim: c.425 is an editorial approximation, not a securely documented end date
episodes.place: Palestine/Galilee; patriarchal authority was not confined to one archaeological site

sources.locator: CTh 16.8.29, 30 May 429, lines 898–900 in opened transcript
sources.supports: Law refers to revenues received after the patriarchs' excessus/cessation and redirects annual synagogue payments to imperial officials/treasury.
sources.limits: It is strong documentary evidence that the law presupposes the patriarchal office's cessation by 429, but is not a precise date or narrative of abolition. It does not date completion of the Jerusalem Talmud or prove learning ceased.

sources.consulted: Relevant excerpt on conflated dates read; exact repository landing URL not captured
sources.locator: Discussion of 415 law, end of patriarchate, and traditional c.425 Yerushalmi dating
sources.supports: Explains that these dates are often linked by inference and that the evidence is sparse; argues against treating them as one securely dated event.
sources.limits: Secondary argument; not itself a dated primary record.

episodes.assessment: Keep 425 only as a qualified editorial boundary. The 429 constitution is the clearest consulted primary evidence referring retrospectively to the patriarchs' cessation; it does not establish the exact year.

crossEpisodeNotes: Imperial constitutions record prescribed norms and officials' duties, not compliance rates or uniform local experience.
CTh 16.8.9 (393), 16.8.14 (399), 16.8.17 (404), 16.8.22 (415), and 16.8.25–29 (423–429) have distinct recipients and scopes. Do not flatten them into a single policy trajectory.
Where only an abstract or search excerpt was accessed, the record says so; those extracts are not treated as full-text consultation.
No source consulted licenses precise population totals, a uniform Jewish communal response, or exact local implementation.
